1.pericope_label: The purpose of the signs declared, and the reproof sent to Pharaoh

schools.summary: Gill notes that some render the clause though I have hardened his heart, since as it stands it reads more like a reason for Moses not to go than for going. Calvin will have none of the softening. God says he hardened the heart in order to show forth these miracles, for if Pharaoh had yielded immediately the contest would have been superfluous — what would be the object of contending with a conquered and prostrate enemy? The obstinacy of the tyrant in so often provoking God opened the way to more miracles, as fire is produced by the collision of flint and iron. Calvin adds that this refutes the notion that the heart was hardened only as the miracles were set before his eyes: Moses does not say it was hardened by the sight of the signs, but that it pleased God in this manner to manifest his power, from which we gather that whatever occurred was predestinated by the sure counsel of God. On the purpose toward Israel he observes that God regarded his own people more than the Egyptians, as the next words show: far more abundant material for thanksgiving was afforded by their having seen God's arm stretched forth so often from heaven and with so many prodigies, whereas had they been redeemed by any ordinary method the praise due to God would soon have been forgotten. It is required of the fathers, who had been eye-witnesses of the signs, that they be diligent in teaching their children, so that the recollection of God's mercies should flourish through all ages. Gill widens the address to the whole nation: not of Moses' own sons and grandsons only, since Moses here, as Aben Ezra observes, stood in the stead of Israel.

Henry begins with Moses rather than with Pharaoh. We may well suppose him much astonished both at Pharaoh's obstinacy and at God's severity, and at a loss to conceive what the contest would come to; here God tells him what he designed — not only Israel's release but the magnifying of his own name, in writings which shall continue to the world's end. The ten plagues had to be inflicted, he says, that they might be recorded as proofs of two things: of God's overruling power in the kingdom of nature, his authority to use the creatures either as servants to his justice or sufferers by it; and of his victorious power over the kingdom of Satan.

Clarke softens the hardening: God suffered Pharaoh's natural obstinacy to prevail, that he might have further opportunities of showing forth his eternal power and Godhead. Of the record to be handed down he says it was not to crush the poor worm Pharaoh that God wrought such wonders, but to convince his enemies to the end of the world that no cunning or power can prevail against him. Wesley takes up Henry's conclusion in the same words: these plagues are standing monuments of the greatness of God, the happiness of the church and the sinfulness of sin, and standing monitors not to provoke the Lord to jealousy nor to strive with our Maker — the benefit of the instruction sufficiently balancing the expense.

Ellicott presses the servants' share of the hardening. They too had first hardened their own hearts, and so deserved a penal hardening; had they allowed the miracles their full natural effect they would have been convinced that resistance was useless and would have impressed their views upon Pharaoh. Keil supplies the ground of the reproof that follows: since Pharaoh had already acknowledged, under the previous plague, that Jehovah was righteous, his crime was now placed still more strongly before him in the question, how long wilt thou refuse to humble thyself before me?

debates.question: In what sense did God harden Pharaoh's heart?

positions.position: God suffered his natural obstinacy to prevail, giving him up to his own stubborn heart
a penal hardening deserved by servants who had first hardened themselves
not merely the effect of the signs on his mind — it pleased God so to manifest his power, and all of it was predestinated by his sure counsel
the clause may even be rendered though I have hardened his heart

themes: I have hardened his heart, and the heart of his servants
that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son
that ye may know how that I am the LORD

3.pericope_label: The locusts threatened, and Moses turns and goes out from Pharaoh

schools.summary: Gill takes the threat at its face, that the plague announced was the locusts. Calvin reads the question how long as a measure of the man's impiety, since though he had seen his kingdom stripped of part of its corn he does not fear for the rest; and because plagues vanquish even the worst natures, it was marvellous that a king smitten eight times should still be unwilling to yield, as if he were in safety and unaffected by any injury. From this Calvin draws what the rods of God are for: that we may return from the indulgence of our lusts to submission; those neither tamed nor bent by fear of punishment struggle against God with a brazen brow. He marks the choice of instrument as a further insult: God collects and arms a host of vile insects, that he may insultingly overcome this indomitable tyrant with all his forces; and the ingratitude of Egypt deserved it, since it was too great an indignity that the posterity of Joseph should be persecuted in the very country which, little more than two hundred and fifty years before, he had preserved from famine. On the departure Calvin makes it a token of indignation, as though Moses, worn out with the perverseness of the tyrant, had withdrawn without bidding him farewell — and though otherwise of a mild disposition, he had to adopt this peremptory harshness as a reproof of the arrogance with which the tyrant spat in the face of heaven. Gill offers the alternatives for the eye of the earth — the appearance and colour of the earth, or the eye of a man unable to see the ground for what lay between — and then reports the Targum of Onkelos, which reads it as the eye of the sun of the earth, so that its rays should not reach the ground; Abarbinel takes it so too, and Gill adds from Pliny that locusts came sometimes in such multitudes as to darken the sun.

Clarke turns the reproof into an argument. Had it been impossible for Pharaoh, under all the preceding plagues, to humble himself, could God have addressed him in such language? There was always a time, he says, when he might have relented, and it was because he hardened his heart at such times that God is said to harden him — to give him up to his own stubborn heart; and had he relented earlier the same gracious ends would have been reached by other means. On the locusts he gives most space to Shaw, who watched swarms in Barbary: the young brood, still worm-like, formed a compact body of more than a furlong square and marched directly forward over trees, walls and houses, and the trenches the inhabitants dug and filled with water or fire were filled up and quenched by infinite swarms succeeding one another, the rear pressing so close that retreat was impossible. Of their filling the houses he quotes Shaw again, that they entered our very houses and bed-chambers like so many thieves. Wesley puts the reproof shortly: it is justly expected of the greatest of men that they humble themselves before the great God — for those who will not humble themselves, God will humble.

Ellicott adds the point that matters for Egypt: locusts are not indigenous there but only occasional visitants, and must always enter from some other country. Beside Clarke's account of the houses he sets Joel, that they shall climb upon the houses and enter in at the windows like a thief. On the departure he sees no anger in it, only that Moses did not wait to see what effect his menace would have, since he knew Pharaoh would not yet fear the Lord. Keil takes the phrase they shall cover the eye of the earth for a figure peculiar to the Pentateuch, resting on the ancient and poetic idea that the earth, with its covering of plants, looks up at man; to render it surface destroys the figure, and face is better.

debates.question: What does the eye of the earth mean?

positions.position: a poetic figure: the earth with its covering of plants looks up at man, so face is a better rendering than surface
the eye is the sun, whose rays the swarm shuts out — so the Targum of Onkelos and Abarbinel

debates.question: Why did Moses turn and go out?

positions.position: from indignation — worn out with the tyrant’s perverseness, he withdrew without bidding him farewell, as a reproof
no anger in it: he simply did not wait to see the effect of his menace, knowing Pharaoh would not yet fear the Lord

themes: how long wilt thou refuse to humble thyself before me
they shall cover the face of the earth
he turned himself, and went out from Pharaoh

7.pericope_label: The servants plead, and Pharaoh will let the men go but not the families

schools.summary: Calvin reads the courtiers severely. They had been obstinate in common with their king, and by their servile flattery had blinded him more and more; now, conquered by their calamities, they seek to mitigate his fury — not because they had returned to their senses, but because they feel themselves overcome by the hand of God and their strength to resist gone. On Pharaoh's wish for the Lord to be with them he makes it an ironical sneer by which he insults God and them together — you boast that God is on your side; experience will prove it, if I let you go — setting himself up as the supreme judge of their departure, and denying that God is able to aid his people against the king's power. Gill thinks the same words mockery: let the Lord you talk of be with you if he will, and let him deliver you if he can, since I shall let you go with your children as soon as never. On the demand itself Gill explains why both ends of the family were needed: the old to guide and instruct in the business of sacrifice, as heads of their families, and the young to be present, that they might be trained up and inured to such services.

Clarke opens on the servants' complaint, noting that there is no noun in the text, so that the pronoun may refer to the Israelites, to the plague they were under, or to Moses and Aaron as the instruments of it; the Vulgate turns it, how long shall we suffer this scandal? He argues that the demand should not have struck the Egyptians as strange, since their own religious assemblies were attended by men, women and children alike. His instance is from Herodotus, who describes the chief of the six annual Egyptian feasts, at Bubastis in honour of Neith or Diana: they go thither by water in boats, men, women and children, some of the women playing on castanets and some of the men upon flutes; and the inhabitants assured him that at one such festival not fewer than seven hundred thousand assembled, without reckoning the children. The parallel is too striking, he says, to pass unnoticed. He calls Pharaoh's wish a curse — may your God be as surely with you as I shall let you go — and observes what the king really calculated: he knew that if the men left their families behind they would infallibly return, whereas if he let them take their families they would undoubtedly escape. Wesley draws the lesson from the restriction: Satan does all he can to hinder those who serve God themselves from bringing their children in to serve him, being a sworn enemy to early piety.

Ellicott traces a widening effect through the chapters: the magicians had said this is the finger of God, some of the people had feared the word of the Lord and housed their servants and cattle, and now the very officers of the court believed the words of Moses would come true. He rejects the supposition that they meant the men only, calling it pure conjecture, since the word they use is not the word of the later verse and would cover women and children; being mostly rich landowners who dreaded ruin, they would intend to counsel entire submission. On Pharaoh's later reproach he denies any ground for it: Moses and Aaron had always demanded the release of the entire nation, and nations are composed of women and children as essentially as of adult males. Keil follows the recall closely: Moses, having announced the plague and left, was fetched back with Aaron at the servants' urging and asked how many wanted to go; he required the whole nation without regard to age or sex, the wives being included in the we.

debates.question: What did the courtiers mean by let the men go?

positions.position: the whole nation — the word used is not that of the later verse and covers women and children; they intended entire submission
they were beaten rather than converted, seeking only to mitigate the king’s fury

debates.question: What did Pharaoh mean by let the LORD be so with you?

a curse — may your God be as surely with you as I shall let you go
an ironical sneer insulting God and them together, denying that God can aid his people against the king

12.pericope_label: The east wind brings the locusts, and they devour what the hail had left

schools.summary: Calvin makes much of the rod. The stretching forth of the hand is a token of power and the rod was given him as a royal sceptre, as if God had made him his vicegerent and subjected to him sea, earth and air; but that he may sink into the character of a minister, Moses does not say the locusts came up at his command, and gives the glory of the operation to the Lord alone. He adds that Moses neither created the locusts nor attracted them by the stirring of his rod: they were divinely brought by the east wind, though so sudden a gathering occurred contrary to the order of nature. Gill says they were raised by the wind where they had been generated, and were in a wonderful manner multiplied by the power of God; and he takes the words about covering the whole earth for the very thing that distinguished this plague. Numbers enough to darken the air have been known before and since, lighting first on one spot and then another; but never such an instance as this, that they should come in so large a body and at once light and spread and settle over a whole country.

Henry reads the stretched-out hand as a summons: God bids Moses beckon them, for they came at a call, and Moses ascribes it not to his own hand but to the rod of God, the instituted sign of his presence — and a formidable army of horse and foot might more easily have been resisted than this host of insects. With Wesley he closes on the ownership of the ground: the earth God has given to the children of men, yet when he pleases he can disturb their possession and send locusts to force them out; herbs grow for the service of man, yet those contemptible insects shall be not merely his fellow-commoners but shall eat the bread out of his mouth.

Clarke denies that any new creation was needed: God had no need to create new swarms, since locusts abounded in those countries at that season, and all that was requisite was such a wind as would bring the existing ones over the land — the miracle lying in bringing them at the appointed time, in causing the proper wind to blow, and in taking them away after a similar manner. Wesley says the east wind brought them from Arabia, where they are in great numbers, and that God miraculously increased them.

Keil rejects the Septuagint's south wind, and Bochart with it. Although swarms are generally brought into Egypt from Libya or Ethiopia by a south wind, they are sometimes brought by the east wind out of Arabia, as Denon has observed. He finds two miracles in the manner of it: the wind blew a day and a night before bringing them, which showed they came from a great distance and proved that the omnipotence of Jehovah reached far beyond the borders of Egypt; and the extent of the swarm was unparalleled, whereas ordinary swarms are confined to particular districts. Ellicott explains why the translators went wrong — locusts most commonly enter Egypt from the south, being bred in Nubia or Abyssinia — but insists the Hebrew is undoubtedly an east wind. On the extent he doubts the literal reading, since universal expressions are continually used by the sacred writers where less than universality is meant, though he allows a general visitation: Egypt extends above five hundred miles from north to south, and no column of locusts of such dimensions is recorded in history, so he supposes it may have been confined to the Delta and the neighbourhood of Memphis — which even so would have covered seven thousand square miles, an area nearly equal to Wales.

debates.question: Were the locusts created for the occasion or only brought?

positions.position: only brought — locusts abounded already, and the miracle lay in the timing and the wind
brought by the wind, but God miraculously increased them
neither created nor drawn by the rod, yet so sudden a gathering was contrary to the order of nature

debates.question: How literally should all the land of Egypt be taken?

positions.position: perhaps only the Delta and the neighbourhood of Memphis: no recorded swarm has covered five hundred miles
literally — this is the very thing that distinguished the plague, that one body settled over a whole country at once

before them there were no such locusts as they

16.pericope_label: Pharaoh confesses, the west wind clears the locusts, and his heart is hardened

schools.summary: Gill marks the reversal: he who a few hours before had driven them from his presence now hastens to call them, and sends messengers to fetch them with all speed; and of the plea he notes that the request is made to Moses and not to the Lord, Moses having been made a god to Pharaoh. Calvin allows that the confession flowed from a deceitful heart yet was not altogether feigned, since God extorted the cry from a man conscious of his sin. He distinguishes two kinds of hypocrite — those who deceive designedly, and those who beguile themselves, having a terror of God's judgments while they cherish iniquity in the heart — and puts Pharaoh in the second class, as one who had no intention of deceiving God or Moses, but who, not examining himself, did not sincerely confess his sin. He grants him one virtue, that it was no ordinary humiliation in a powerful king to beg forgiveness of an obscure and despised individual. But by desiring that only this present death be removed, he shows he does not much care for an entire reconciliation with God, the wicked being usually indifferent to his hatred or favour and dreading only his hand. Calvin explains why Moses went out of the city to pray: the king was not worthy that the name of God should be invoked in his presence, and Moses prayed not because he thought him converted but to open God's way for the contests that remained. On the sea's name he derives it either from the reeds with which it abounds or from its whirlwinds, since the word is used in Scripture in both senses, so that it might be rendered either the weedy sea or the tempestuous. Gill closes on the hardening with the plainest reason: God had not yet brought upon Pharaoh all the judgments he designed.

Clarke stands back in astonishment: what a strange case, what a series of softening and hardening, of sinning and repenting; had he not now another opportunity of returning to God? But the love of gain and his own self-will prevailed. On the wind that carried the locusts off he observes that the Hebrew is literally the wind of the sea, blowing from the Mediterranean, which lay north-west of Egypt as the Red Sea lay east; here again God works by natural means, bringing the locusts by one wind and removing them by another. On the sea's name he reports Bruce against the usual derivation: having sailed its whole extent he declares he never saw in it a weed of any kind, and supposes the name comes rather from the vast quantity of coral which grows there as trees do on land. He further supposes the Greek name came from Edom or Esau, whose territories reached its coasts, Edom in Hebrew signifying red. Wesley puts the charge against the confession shortly: Pharaoh desires their prayers that this death only might be taken away, not this sin — he deprecates the plague of locusts, not the plague of a hard heart.

Ellicott notes that the phrase hasted to call is new and marks extreme urgency, the visitation being felt as far more severe than any before it: it destroyed the remaining harvest of grain and fruit, and must have brought famine but for the Egyptian granaries. He reckons the confession an improvement upon the earlier one, as acknowledging a double fault, against the Lord and against you, and as free from any attempt to shift the blame upon others; it was probably sincere at the time, though the feeling was short-lived. On the sea's name he takes the weed sense historically, supposing the name was given because in the time of Moses the north-western recess of the gulf communicated with a marshy tract abounding in aquatic plants. Keil observes that Pharaoh calls the locusts death, as bringing death and ruin to the country.

positions.position: probably sincere at the time, and an improvement on the earlier confession, though short-lived
not feigned, but the confession of a man who beguiles himself: he did not examine himself, and cared only that the punishment be removed

debates.question: Why is it called the sea of weeds?

positions.position: from the reeds it abounds in, or else from its whirlwinds — the word bears both senses
from the marshy tract, full of aquatic plants, with which its north-western recess then communicated
neither — Bruce sailed its whole extent and saw no weed at all; the name comes from its coral

21.pericope_label: The darkness that might be felt, and light in the dwellings of Israel

schools.summary: Calvin notes first that this plague comes without warning, because Pharaoh had deceitfully broken his promise and so must be suddenly overtaken, that he might feel in the darkness the avenging hand he had despised; nor would menaces have alarmed him, as appears when he afterwards heard of the death of the first-born unmoved. He holds the darkness so thick that it might be felt by the hand. Turning from the manner to the meaning, he observes that no blessing is more common to all men than light, which the humblest enjoy no less than kings, so that it was a terrible judgment that the world should be enlightened by the sun while the Egyptians, though possessing sight, were plunged in darkness. And that the vengeance might be neither obscure nor doubtful, the cause could not be assigned to an eclipse, both on account of its density and the time it lasted, which Moses expressly notes. Gill dates the three days as the eleventh, twelfth and thirteenth of the month Abib.

Henry and Wesley describe it as total. Not only were the lights of heaven clouded, but their fires and candles were put out by the damps which caused it, for they saw not one another; and the Jewish tradition is that in the darkness they were terrified by apparitions of evil spirits, or rather by the dreadful sounds these made, or — no less frightful — by the horrors of their own consciences. It continued three days, six nights, says bishop Hall, in one; no man rose from his place, and such terror seized them that few dared go from the chair to the bed — and now Pharaoh had time to consider, if he would have improved it. They take the darkness that might be felt both ways: felt in its causes by their fingers' ends, so thick were the fogs, and in its effects by their eyes, which were pricked with pain and made the more sore by rubbing. Of the light in Goshen they note that it was not confined there but reached the dwellings of Israelites dispersed among the Egyptians; and Wesley draws out what was not done with it — during those three days they might have escaped and asked Pharaoh no leave, but God would bring them out with a high hand, not by stealth or in haste.

Clarke supposes a superabundance of aqueous vapours floating in the atmosphere, so thick as to prevent the sun's rays from penetrating — an extraordinarily thick mist miraculously brought on. He sets beside the scene the description in the Wisdom of Solomon: the Egyptians shut up in their houses, prisoners of darkness, fettered with the bonds of a long night, troubled with strange apparitions; and no power of the fire could give them light, only there appeared a fire kindled of itself very dreadful. Of the distinction made for Israel he reads it as an argument to the Egyptians, that the darkness was produced by God's power and sent in judgment.

Ellicott will not press the phrase so far: the Hebrew is one shall grasp darkness, and our version, with the Septuagint and Vulgate, gives the true meaning, but the idea is an exaggeration of that instinctive feeling which makes us speak of thick darkness. He alone resists the received picture of the three days. The darkness was absolute, he grants, and no one quitted his house; but it is not necessary to suppose they had no artificial light, or ceased to move from chamber to chamber, and when Millington imagines them all sitting glued to their seats this savours of over-literalism. What the writer intends, he says, is that all business and intercourse was suspended, and that no one left the house he was in when the darkness began. Keil, reading on, notes that at the demand which followed Pharaoh, with the hardness suspended over him by God, fell into such wrath that he threatened Moses with death if he appeared again.

positions.position: total — fires and candles put out, no man daring to move from the chair to the bed
over-literalism: they may well have had artificial light and moved from room to room; what ceased was business and intercourse outside the house

debates.question: What is meant by darkness that may be felt?

positions.position: thick vapours felt by the fingers, and pain in the eyes
an exaggeration of the instinctive feeling behind the phrase thick darkness, confirmed by the general voice of mankind

themes: darkness which may be felt
they saw not one another, neither rose any from his place
all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings

24.pericope_label: The last bargain refused, and Moses dismissed on pain of death

schools.summary: Calvin raises a difficulty the others pass over: if no one rose from his place for three days, how could Pharaoh send for Moses at all? To answer that the messengers went after the darkness dispersed will not do, since as often as God withdrew his hand the tyrant cast aside his fear and returned to his ferocity. His own opinion is that while the exigency still pressed, and Pharaoh feared the darkness might never lift, he took counsel how to appease Moses; and that none rose from his place is spoken hyperbolically, of their ceasing from the occupations that required light. On the refusal he admires the manner as much as the matter: Moses repudiates all exceptions as if he authoritatively demanded of the king what God had enjoined, and by this austere and abrupt way of speaking evidenced his courage; leaving not a hair in the king's power, he asserts the indivisible right of God alone. Of the hardening he says flatly that God was the author of the obduracy — not because he inspired obstinacy into a heart otherwise disposed to docility, but because he gave over to Satan a reprobate wilfully devoted to his own destruction — and professes astonishment at the sophists who substitute the word allow, and by that evasion escape so plain a statement. Of the dismissal he observes that Moses set all this froth at naught, and that the king, carried away by fury, prophesied against his own mind, since God returned upon his own head what he threatened against another. Gill, taking the last words absolutely, thinks Moses knew by a spirit of prophecy that he should be sent to Pharaoh no more.

Clarke finds the demand as avaricious as it is cruel, and reckons its effect: had six hundred thousand men, besides women and children, gone three days into the wilderness without their cattle, they must inevitably have perished, being without milk for their little ones and animal food for themselves where little substitute could be found — whence it is evident that Pharaoh intended the total destruction of the Israelitish host. He supplies the plain reason for the refusal: the law was not yet given and the ordinances concerning the kinds of sacrifice were not known, so that what animals and how many God should require even Moses could not as yet tell, and he therefore insists on taking the whole of their herds. On the hardening he keeps to his own account: God had another miracle to work for the conviction of the Egyptians, and till that was wrought he permitted the natural obstinacy of Pharaoh's haughty heart to have its full sway. He thinks this interview likely to have been the last, supposing the words of the next chapter were spoken now, and that Pharaoh's later summons implies no more than a message sent. Wesley holds instead that the conference did not break off until Moses went out in great anger.

Ellicott reads the offer as a hold rather than a snare: Pharaoh yields another point but not all, and the cattle serve his purpose as well as the families, since if the Israelites depart without their herds they will be sure to return for them. On the refusal he gives two reasons — the cattle are theirs and not Pharaoh's, and they are God's, all to the last head if he requires it; the people will only be told with what they must serve the Lord when they come to the place where they are to serve him. He judges the dismissal by the manners of the court: the address is rude, fierce and uncourteous, and that a Pharaoh of that dynasty should so speak implies very uncommon excitement, the Pharaohs of this polished period being generally as imperturbable as Chinese mandarins; the king had persuaded himself he could bring Moses to a compromise, and at last despaired of it.

there shall not an hoof be left behind
